set1.io: 3 — Describe phage therapy
set1.q: Why was phage therapy abandoned in the West after the 1920s and 1930s?
opts: Antibiotic therapy emerged
Correct: phage therapy was explored in eastern Europe in the 1920s and 1930s but abandoned in the West once antibiotics, such as penicillin in the 1940s, became available.
Phages were found to infect humans
Phages do not infect human cells; the West dropped phage therapy when antibiotics emerged.
It was banned as too dangerous
No ban is the reason given; the West abandoned it with the emergence of antibiotic therapy.
Phages could not be grown
Phages could be produced; the reason was the arrival of antibiotics such as penicillin.

set1.io: 3 — Describe phage therapy
set1.q: In a tailed bacteriophage, which structure holds the genome?
opts: The baseplate
The baseplate sits at the end of the tail and attaches to the cell; the genome is in the head.
The long tail fibers
The tail fibers grip the bacterial surface; the genome is packed in the head.
The head
Correct: the genome, shown as DNA, is packed in the head; the tail tube, sheath, baseplate and long tail fibers deliver it into the bacterium.
The tail sheath
The tail sheath surrounds the tail tube; the genome is packed in the head.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set1.q: Which patient fits the high-risk group for which many dentists still give antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work?
opts: A patient with well-controlled asthma
Asthma is not a high-risk scenario for dental prophylaxis; prosthetic heart valves and prior endocarditis are.
A patient with a prosthetic heart valve
Correct: dental prophylaxis is now limited to a few high-risk scenarios, such as a prosthetic heart valve or a history of endocarditis.
A healthy patient having a routine cleaning
Healthy patients do not need prophylaxis; it is limited to high-risk scenarios such as a prosthetic heart valve.
A patient with seasonal allergies
Allergies do not raise the risk dental prophylaxis protects against; a prosthetic heart valve does.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set1.q: Which Gram-positive organism is listed among the superbugs for its resistance to vancomycin?
opts: Enterococcus
Correct: vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus is on the superbug list, alongside vancomycin-resistant and vancomycin-intermediate Staphylococcus aureus.
Lactobacillus
Lactobacillus is a beneficial bacterium used as a probiotic; the vancomycin-resistant superbug listed is Enterococcus.
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniae is not the vancomycin-resistant organism on the list; that is Enterococcus.
Listeria monocytogenes
Listeria is not on the superbug list; the organism named for vancomycin resistance is Enterococcus.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set1.q: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is frequently resistant to ciprofloxacin and erythromycin. Which of these antibiotics typically remains active against it?
opts: Ciprofloxacin
Ciprofloxacin susceptibility collapses in methicillin-resistant strains; vancomycin remains active against them.
None of the listed drugs
One of them is: vancomycin remains active against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
Vancomycin

Correct: on a hospital antibiogram vancomycin kept full activity against methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant strains alike, while ciprofloxacin and erythromycin susceptibility dropped sharply in the resistant ones.
Erythromycin
Erythromycin is one of the drugs methicillin-resistant strains most often resist; vancomycin remains active against them.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set1.q: Which statement about ear infections and antibiotics is accurate?
opts: Every ear infection requires an antibiotic
Not every ear infection needs one; some ear infections do not require an antibiotic.
Ear infections are never caused by bacteria
Some ear infections are bacterial; the point is that some of them do not require an antibiotic, not that none are bacterial.
Ear infections respond only to antivirals
Antivirals are not the standard answer here; the fact is that some ear infections do not need an antibiotic at all.
Some ear infections do not require an antibiotic
Correct: some ear infections do not require an antibiotic, one of the six facts about antibiotic use alongside 'most sore throats do not'.

set1.io: 2 — Describe fecal microbiota transplant (FMT)
set1.q: Why are stool donors screened before fecal microbiota transplant?
opts: To confirm the donor has taken antibiotics
Recent antibiotics would disturb the donor flora; screening is about excluding pathogens.
To reduce the risk of passing on pathogens
Correct: donor screening, similar to blood bank screening, reduces the risk of passing on blood-borne and other pathogens to the recipient.
To match the donor's blood type
Blood type does not matter for stool; screening is to keep pathogens from reaching the recipient.
To find donors who take probiotics
Probiotic use is not the point; screening keeps blood-borne and other pathogens out of the transplant.

set1.io: 4 — Describe other alternative therapies to antibiotic use
set1.q: Which is one of the hypotheses for why herbs and spices are used across cultures?
opts: They sterilize food completely
No spice sterilizes food; the hypothesis is that some kill bacteria and fungi, especially in spoilage.
Some kill bacteria and fungi in food
Correct: one hypothesis is that some herbs and spices kill bacteria and fungi, especially those that spoil food; others are taste, smell and nutrients.
They replace salt as a preservative
Replacing salt is not among the hypotheses; one is that some spices kill the bacteria and fungi that spoil food.
They make food cheaper to produce
Cost is not a listed hypothesis; antimicrobial action against food spoilage is.

set1.io: 2 — Describe fecal microbiota transplant (FMT)
set1.q: What material does a patient receive in a fecal microbiota transplant?
opts: Screened donor stool
Correct: fecal microbiota transplant uses screened donor stool samples, often from stool banks, to restore the patient's gut microflora.
The patient's own blood plasma
Plasma carries antibodies, as in convalescent plasma; fecal microbiota transplant uses screened donor stool.
A purified antibiotic
No antibiotic is given; the material is screened donor stool that restores the gut flora.
A suspension of bacteriophages
Phages are a separate therapy; fecal microbiota transplant uses screened donor stool.

set1.io: 2 — Describe fecal microbiota transplant (FMT)
set1.q: A patient has had three recurrences of Clostridioides difficile infection despite treatment. Which novel therapy is established for preventing further recurrence?
opts: Convalescent plasma
Convalescent plasma gives donor antibodies; fecal microbiota transplant is the therapy researched for Clostridioides difficile.
Fecal microbiota transplant
Correct: fecal microbiota transplant has been specifically researched as a treatment for Clostridioides difficile infection, and preventing recurrence is its established use.
Systemic corticosteroids
Corticosteroids dampen host inflammation and do not restore the gut flora; fecal microbiota transplant is the established therapy for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection.
Plant essential oils
Essential oils have only in vitro antibacterial activity; fecal microbiota transplant is the therapy studied for Clostridioides difficile.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set1.q: Which patients most commonly receive empiric antibiotic therapy?
opts: Healthy patients with no symptoms
Treating people without symptoms would be prophylaxis or overuse; empiric therapy is for sick patients, especially critically ill ones.
Patients whose cultures are already back
Once cultures are back, therapy is directed by the results; empiric therapy is given before they are available.
Only patients with viral infections
Antibiotics do not treat viruses; empiric therapy covers a suspected bacterial infection in a sick patient before results return.
Critically ill or emergent patients
Correct: empiric therapy is common in human and veterinary medicine, especially for critically ill or emergent patients who cannot wait for results.

set1.io: 3 — Describe phage therapy
set1.q: Which regulatory hurdle does phage therapy face in the United States?
opts: Phages are classed as controlled substances
They are not controlled substances; the hurdle is that no phage product is yet approved as a medicine.
Phages are already fully approved for all infections
No phage product has been approved as a medicine for routine use; clearance still needs special routes.
Phages may be sold only as dietary supplements
Phages are not sold as supplements for therapy; the hurdle is that no phage product is yet approved as a medicine.
No phage product is yet approved as a medicine

Correct: bacterial viruses are not yet established as approved medicinal products, so regulatory clearance is a concern; investigational drug status and emergency use authorization are routes around it.

set1.io: 4 — Describe other alternative therapies to antibiotic use
set1.q: Which foods are a common natural source of probiotics?
opts: Fermented foods
Correct: probiotics such as Lactobacillus and Saccharomyces are often found in fermented foods.
Canned vegetables
Canning heats food to kill microbes; the natural probiotic source is fermented foods.
Refined sugar
Sugar carries no beneficial microbes; probiotics are often found in fermented foods.
Pasteurized juice
Pasteurization kills microbes; probiotics come from fermented foods.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set1.q: Which injury is an example of a high-risk trauma for which antimicrobial prophylaxis is used?
opts: A first-degree sunburn
Sunburn does not breach the skin deeply; prophylaxis is for high-risk injuries such as animal bites or penetrating brain injury.
A bruise from a fall
A bruise leaves the skin intact; high-risk injuries such as animal bites are where prophylaxis is used.
An animal bite
Correct: antimicrobial prophylaxis is used in traumatic injuries where the risk of infection is high, such as animal bites or penetrating brain injury.
A closed ankle sprain
A sprain with intact skin carries little infection risk; prophylaxis is for high-risk wounds such as animal bites.

set1.io: 3 — Describe phage therapy
set1.q: What still has to be precisely defined before phage therapy is used routinely?
opts: The color of the phage preparation
Color is not an issue; dose, route, frequency and duration must be defined.
Whether phages infect bacteria
That is settled: phages infect bacteria. The open questions are dose, route, frequency and duration.
Which patients prefer phages to pills
Preference is not the open question; optimal dose, route, frequency and duration are.
The dose, route, frequency and duration
Correct: phage therapy is not a magic bullet: the optimal dose, administration route, frequency and duration of treatment still need to be precisely defined.

set1.io: 3 — Describe phage therapy
set1.q: Which cells do bacteriophages attack?
opts: Only human cells
Phages do not infect human cells; they attack bacteria only.
Bacteria and human cells alike
Phages attack bacteria and no other type of cell, human cells included.
Fungi and parasites
Phages are specific to bacteria; fungi and parasites are not their hosts.
Only bacteria
Correct: phages specifically attack bacteria and no other types of cells, which is why they are attractive as a therapy.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set1.q: Antimicrobial prophylaxis for close contacts is used to prevent the spread of which group of infections?
opts: Tuberculosis, meningitis and pertussis
Correct: prophylaxis to prevent transmission of pathogens to susceptible contacts is used, for example, for tuberculosis, meningitis or pertussis.
Influenza, measles and mumps
These viral illnesses are not what antibacterial contact prophylaxis targets; the examples are tuberculosis, meningitis and pertussis.
Tetanus, botulism and gas gangrene
These are not spread from person to person, so contacts need no prophylaxis; the examples are tuberculosis, meningitis and pertussis.
Acne, cellulitis and impetigo
Skin infections are not the examples given; contact prophylaxis is used for tuberculosis, meningitis and pertussis.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set1.q: In a disk diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) test, what does the clear zone around an antibiotic disk show?
opts: Where the antibiotic was used up
The clear zone is where the drug was concentrated enough to stop growth, not where it ran out.
Growth inhibited by the antibiotic
Correct: the circular zone of inhibition is where the antibiotic diffusing from the paper disk stopped the bacteria growing, showing how effective that drug is.
Bacteria that are resistant to the drug
Resistant bacteria grow right up to the disk; the clear zone is where growth was inhibited.
Contamination from the paper disk
The disk carries antibiotic, not contaminants; the clear ring is the zone of inhibition.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set1.q: Penicillin, vancomycin and azithromycin share which pattern?
opts: Resistance took about a century to appear
It took years, not a century; each drug met resistance within a few years to about two decades of widespread use.
Resistance appeared within years of widespread use
Correct: for each drug, resistance was first detected within a few years to about two decades of its widespread clinical use, a reminder that use selects for resistance.
Resistance appeared before each drug was discovered
Resistance was detected after each drug came into widespread clinical use, not before it was discovered.
Resistance has never been detected to any of them
Resistance has been detected to all three: penicillin, vancomycin and azithromycin each met resistant bacteria after coming into wide use.

set1.io: 4 — Describe other alternative therapies to antibiotic use
set1.q: How does a prebiotic differ from a probiotic?
opts: Prebiotics are antibiotics taken before meals
Prebiotics are not antibiotics; they are fiber-rich foods that feed the gut microflora.
They are two names for the same thing
They differ: prebiotics feed the gut flora, while probiotics are beneficial microbes.
Prebiotics feed gut flora; probiotics are live microbes
Correct: prebiotics are fiber-rich foods that provide nutrients to the gut microflora; probiotics are the beneficial organisms themselves, such as Lactobacillus and Saccharomyces.
Prebiotics are live microbes; probiotics feed them
This reverses them: prebiotics are fiber that nourishes the gut flora, and probiotics are the live beneficial organisms.

set1.io: 3 — Describe phage therapy
set1.q: What kind of genome can a bacteriophage carry?
opts: Both DNA and RNA together
No virus carries both kinds of nucleic acid; a phage has either DNA or RNA as its genome, never both.
DNA only, never RNA
Some phages have RNA; a phage carries DNA or RNA, though never both.
Protein only, with no nucleic acid
Every phage carries nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA; protein forms its coat and tail.
DNA or RNA, never both
Correct: like all viruses, bacteriophages can have DNA or RNA, but never both.

set1.io: 3 — Describe phage therapy
set1.q: Why could phage therapy be more efficient than antibiotics once the infection is cleared?
opts: Phages die off when their host bacteria are gone
Correct: phages target specific bacterial cells and then die off when their host is no longer present, one reason given for greater efficacy than antibiotics.
Phages stay in the body for life
The reverse is claimed: without their host bacteria phages die off.
Phages become antibiotics in the body
Phages do not turn into antibiotics; they replicate on their target and die off when it is gone.
Phages switch to attacking other bacteria
Phages are highly host-specific; once their host is gone they die off rather than switching targets.

set1.io: 4 — Describe other alternative therapies to antibiotic use
set1.q: Which plants are named among the herbs and spices studied for antimicrobial properties?
opts: Garlic, oregano and cinnamon
Correct: the list includes garlic, onion, allspice, oregano, thyme, cinnamon, cumin, basil, ginger, cloves, rosemary and others.
Tobacco, coffee and tea
These are not on the herb and spice list; garlic, oregano and cinnamon are.
Wheat, rice and corn
Grains are not the herbs and spices listed; garlic, oregano and cinnamon are.
Potato, carrot and celery
These vegetables are not on the spice list; garlic, oregano and cinnamon are.

set1.io: 2 — Describe fecal microbiota transplant (FMT)
set1.q: What is the main purpose of fecal microbiota transplant?
opts: Delivering a high-dose antibiotic
No antibiotic is delivered; donor stool restores the gut microflora.
Vaccinating against intestinal viruses
It is not a vaccine; it restores the gut's microbial community from a donor.
Removing all bacteria from the colon
The aim is the reverse: adding a healthy donor community to restore the gut flora.
Restoring a healthy gut microflora
Correct: fecal microbiota transplant gives screened donor stool to realign the patient's gastrointestinal microflora.

set1.io: 4 — Describe other alternative therapies to antibiotic use
set1.q: What is still needed before plant essential oils can be judged as antibacterial treatments?
opts: Better experimental design
Correct: the hypotheses about herbs and spices need better experimental design to test them; in vitro activity alone does not show clinical benefit.
Nothing; they are already standard care
They are not standard care; their activity is in vitro, and better-designed experiments are needed.
Only a lower price
Cost is not the gap; the hypotheses need better experimental design to be tested.
Regulatory approval as antibiotics alone
Approval would follow evidence; what is missing first is better experimental design.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set1.q: Which problem is the main force driving the search for novel antimicrobial therapies?
opts: Antibiotics that cost too much
Price is not the stated driver; antibiotics are losing effectiveness because microbes become resistant to them.
Viruses replacing bacteria as pathogens
Bacteria remain major pathogens; the problem is that more of them resist the antibiotics we have, which is why alternatives are sought.
Antimicrobial resistance

Correct: resistance to antimicrobials and antibiotics heads the list of what drives the need for novel therapies, fed by overuse in agriculture, inappropriate prescribing and patients not finishing treatment.
Shortages of antibiotic raw materials
Supply shortages are not what drives the search; the driver is microbes becoming resistant, fed by overuse and inappropriate prescribing.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set1.q: An antibiotic does not clear a patient's infection. How is this classified among adverse effects of antimicrobials?
opts: An indirect effect on the environment
Environmental effects concern antibiotics in food and water; failure to cure is direct therapeutic failure.
It is not an adverse effect
Therapeutic failure is listed among the direct adverse effects of antimicrobial drugs.
A direct effect: therapeutic failure
Correct: therapeutic failure is grouped with the direct adverse effects, alongside allergy, toxicity and drug-drug interactions.
An indirect effect on the gut flora
Gut flora effects such as Clostridioides difficile infection are indirect; a drug failing to clear the infection is direct therapeutic failure.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set1.q: Which sexually transmitted pathogen is listed among the drug-resistant superbugs?
opts: Herpes simplex virus
A virus is not an antibiotic-resistant superbug; the bacterium listed is Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Correct: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is on the superbug list, with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Pseudomonas.
Treponema pallidum
Treponema pallidum causes syphilis but is not on the superbug list; Neisseria gonorrhoeae is.
Chlamydia trachomatis
Chlamydia is not among the listed superbugs; the sexually transmitted one listed is Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

set1.io: 2 — Describe fecal microbiota transplant (FMT)
set1.q: 'Yellow soup' from old Chinese texts is an early form of which therapy?
opts: Convalescent plasma
Yellow soup was a fecal preparation, not plasma; it is an early fecal microbiota transplant.
Fecal microbiota transplant
Correct: recipes for 'yellow soup', from Ge Hong in the 4th century and Li Shizhen in the 16th, are early forms of fecal microbiota transplant.
Phage therapy
Phage therapy dates from the 20th century; yellow soup is an early fecal microbiota transplant.
An herbal essential oil
Yellow soup was a fecal preparation, an early form of fecal microbiota transplant, not a plant oil.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set1.q: Clinically inappropriate antibiotic prescribing creates the need for which program?
opts: Routine prophylaxis for every patient
Blanket prophylaxis would add to overuse; prophylaxis is reserved for defined high-risk situations, and the response to bad prescribing is stewardship.
Replacing all antibiotics with vaccines
Vaccines prevent some infections but do not replace antibiotics; the response to inappropriate prescribing is antimicrobial stewardship.
Antimicrobial stewardship
Correct: inappropriate prescriptions lead to the need for antimicrobial stewardship, which works through clinician and patient education.
Mandatory antibiotic rationing
Rationing is not the answer named; the response is stewardship, educating clinicians and patients so antibiotics are used only when needed.

set2.io: 3 — Describe phage therapy
set2.q: What is a bacteriophage?
opts: An antibiotic made by fungi
Fungal products such as penicillin are antibiotics; a bacteriophage is a virus that attacks bacteria.
A virus that infects bacteria
Correct: bacteriophages, or phages, are very small viruses that specifically attack bacteria and no other types of cells.
A white blood cell that eats bacteria
A phagocyte eats bacteria; a bacteriophage is a virus that infects bacteria.
A bacterium that infects viruses
It is the other way round: a bacteriophage is a virus that infects bacteria.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set2.q: The ESKAPE pathogens top the lists of which kind of infection?
opts: Foodborne outbreaks at restaurants
Foodborne outbreaks have other leading causes; the ESKAPE pathogens are known for nosocomial, hospital-acquired infections.
Childhood vaccine-preventable diseases
The vaccine-preventable diseases are a different list; the ESKAPE pathogens lead the causes of hospital-acquired infections.
Sexually transmitted infections
Sexually transmitted infections are not what the ESKAPE group names; it leads the causes of nosocomial infections.
Hospital-acquired infections
Correct: the ESKAPE pathogens top the lists of organisms causing nosocomial, that is hospital-acquired, infections.

set2.io: 4 — Describe other alternative therapies to antibiotic use
set2.q: Lactobacillus and Saccharomyces are used as probiotics. Which describes them correctly?
opts: Two harmful superbugs
Both are beneficial organisms used as probiotics, not drug-resistant pathogens.
A beneficial bacterium and a beneficial fungus
Correct: Lactobacillus is a beneficial bacterium and Saccharomyces a beneficial fungus (a yeast), both often found in fermented foods.
Two beneficial viruses
Neither is a virus: Lactobacillus is a bacterium and Saccharomyces is a fungus.
A beneficial fungus and a beneficial bacterium
The order is reversed: Lactobacillus is the bacterium and Saccharomyces the fungus.

set2.io: 3 — Describe phage therapy
set2.q: What property makes bacteriophages a possible option against highly antibiotic-resistant bacteria?
opts: Broad activity against all microbes
Phages are narrow, not broad; their high host specificity is what makes them an option.
Ability to infect human cells
Phages do not infect human cells; their value is high specificity for their bacterial hosts.
Resistance to every antibiotic
Antibiotics do not act on phages anyway; the useful property is their high host specificity.
High host specificity
Correct: phages exhibit high host specificity, so they could attack highly resistant clinical strains while leaving other cells alone.

set2.io: 4 — Describe other alternative therapies to antibiotic use
set2.q: Which non-antimicrobial option gives a patient antibodies from other people?
opts: Intravenous immunoglobulin
Correct: intravenous immunoglobulin G and convalescent plasma supply ready-made antibodies from donors, a non-antimicrobial option.
Systemic corticosteroids
Corticosteroids reduce the host's inflammation and supply no antibodies.
Prebiotic fiber
Prebiotics are fiber that feeds the gut flora; they contain no antibodies.
A probiotic yeast
A probiotic yeast such as Saccharomyces adds a beneficial organism, not antibodies.

set2.io: 3 — Describe phage therapy
set2.q: Why might phage therapy disturb the patient's microbiome less than an antibiotic?
opts: Its antimicrobial spectrum is narrow
Correct: a narrow antimicrobial spectrum would help preserve the patient's existing microbiome, because only the target bacteria are attacked.
It kills every bacterium quickly
Killing every bacterium would harm the microbiome most; phages are narrow, which is why they spare it.
It is given only by mouth
Route is not the reason; the narrow spectrum is what spares the microbiome.
It strengthens the patient's antibodies
Phages do not work through the patient's antibodies; their narrow spectrum spares the microbiome.

set2.io: 2 — Describe fecal microbiota transplant (FMT)
set2.q: What do veterinarians call fecal microbiota transplant?
opts: Transduction
Transduction is gene transfer by a bacteriophage; the veterinary name for fecal transplant is transfaunation.
Transfection
Transfection is putting nucleic acid into cells in the laboratory; the veterinary term is transfaunation.
Transformation
Transformation is bacteria taking up free DNA; fecal transplant in animals is transfaunation.
Transfaunation
Correct: veterinarians call it 'transfaunation', and it works for animals too.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set2.q: How has antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures changed?
opts: It is now limited to a few high-risk patients
Correct: many dentists' policies now limit dental prophylaxis to a few high-risk scenarios, such as prosthetic heart valves or prior endocarditis.
It is now given to every dental patient
The trend is the opposite: dental prophylaxis is now limited to a few high-risk patients.
It has been replaced by probiotics
Probiotics have not replaced it; dental prophylaxis is simply restricted to a few high-risk patients.
It is now given only after the procedure
Timing is not the change; the change is that it is limited to a few high-risk patients.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set2.alt: Two agar plates side by side, each with several white antibiotic disks; the right plate shows wide clear rings around its disks while the left plate shows growth close to its disks.
set2.slide: Disk diffusion plates, Escherichia coli (left) and Staphylococcus aureus (right).
set2.q: In these disk diffusion plates, what do the wide clear rings around the disks on the right-hand plate indicate?
opts: That organism is inhibited by those antibiotics
Correct: wide zones of inhibition mean the antibiotics stopped that organism growing around the disks; growth close to the disks means little effect.
That organism is resistant to those antibiotics
Resistance shows as growth up to the disk; wide clear rings mean the organism was inhibited.
The plate was not inoculated with bacteria
The plate is covered in growth outside the rings; the clear rings are zones of inhibition around the disks.
The disks carried no antibiotic
Blank disks would leave no rings; the clear zones show the antibiotic diffusing out and inhibiting growth.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set2.q: Roughly how many antibiotics are on the market today?
opts: Over 100
Correct: there are over 100 antibiotics on the market, and resistance by microbes is still becoming more prevalent.
About 10
There are far more than 10; over 100 antibiotics are on the market, and resistance is spreading anyway.
About 30
There are many more than 30; over 100 antibiotics are on the market today.
Over 1,000
The number is over 100, not over 1,000; even so, resistance is becoming more prevalent.

set2.io: 3 — Describe phage therapy
set2.q: Which is a drawback of phage therapy in a resource-limited healthcare setting?
opts: Identifying the causative agent can be slow and costly
Correct: phage therapy needs the causative agent identified, and that can be time-consuming and cost-prohibitive in resource-limited settings.
Phages cannot survive outside a hospital
Survival outside hospitals is not the issue; identifying the causative organism can be slow and costly there.
Phages work only in cold climates
Climate is not the problem; identifying the causative agent can be time-consuming and cost-prohibitive.
Phages are broad-spectrum and kill the microbiome
Phages are narrow, which spares the microbiome; the drawback is the cost and time of identifying the agent.

set2.io: 2 — Describe fecal microbiota transplant (FMT)
set2.q: Which intestinal parasites are stool donors screened for?
opts: None; parasites are not screened
Parasites are screened: Giardia and Cryptosporidium are on the list.
Giardia and Cryptosporidium
Correct: donor stool is tested for the parasites Giardia and Cryptosporidium, along with Clostridioides difficile and blood-borne infections.
Tapeworm and pinworm only
The parasites named in donor screening are Giardia and Cryptosporidium.
Plasmodium and Leishmania
These are blood and tissue parasites not on the donor list; Giardia and Cryptosporidium are.

set2.io: 3 — Describe phage therapy
set2.q: Which safety concern is raised about bacteriophages used as therapy?
opts: The phage could infect the patient's own cells
Phages attack only bacteria; the concern raised is that a phage could transfer DNA into its host bacterium.
The phage could turn into a fungus
A virus cannot become a fungus; the concern is DNA transfer into the host bacterium.
The phage could make antibiotics stronger
That would be a benefit, not a concern; the safety question is DNA transfer to the host bacterium.
The phage could transfer DNA into the bacterium
Correct: one worry is gene transfer, a phage moving DNA into its host bacterium, which could carry traits such as toxin or resistance genes.

set2.io: 3 — Describe phage therapy
set2.q: By which two life cycles can bacteriophages replicate?
opts: Sporulation and germination
Sporulation is how some bacteria survive harsh conditions; phages replicate by lytic or lysogenic cycles.
Conjugation and transformation
Conjugation and transformation are ways bacteria exchange DNA; phages replicate by lytic or lysogenic cycles.
Lytic and lysogenic
Correct: phages replicate by a lytic cycle, which bursts the host bacterium, or a lysogenic cycle, which folds the phage genome into the host.
Binary fission and budding
Binary fission and budding are how bacteria and yeasts reproduce; phages use lytic or lysogenic cycles.

set2.io: 4 — Describe other alternative therapies to antibiotic use
set2.q: What kind of antibacterial activity have plant essential oils shown?
opts: Activity only against viruses
The activity described is antibacterial, and in vitro; viruses are not the point.
No activity of any kind
They do show antibacterial activity in vitro, though clinical use still needs better-designed testing.
Activity in laboratory (in vitro) studies
Correct: plant essential oils have shown antibacterial activity in vitro; better experimental design is still needed to test what that means for people.
Proven cures in large clinical trials
The evidence is laboratory (in vitro) activity; better-designed studies are still needed, so cures are not established.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set2.q: Which pair are both drug-resistant forms of Staphylococcus aureus on the superbug list?
opts: Spore-forming and acid-fast
Staphylococcus aureus is neither spore-forming nor acid-fast; the resistant forms listed are methicillin-resistant and vancomycin-resistant.
Methicillin-resistant and vancomycin-resistant
Correct: the list includes methicillin-resistant (MRSA) and vancomycin-resistant or vancomycin-intermediate Staphylococcus aureus (VRSA, VISA).
Penicillin-sensitive and tetracycline-sensitive
Sensitive strains are not resistant forms; the resistant forms listed are methicillin-resistant and vancomycin-resistant.
Coagulase-negative and catalase-negative
Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase and catalase positive; the resistant forms listed are methicillin-resistant and vancomycin-resistant.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set2.q: A critically ill patient with suspected sepsis is started on antibiotics before blood culture results return. What happens to the regimen once results are available?
opts: A second empiric drug is always added
Adding drugs automatically is not the rule; the empiric regimen is adjusted to the results.
It is adjusted to fit the results
Correct: empiric therapy is started on experience and antibiograms and then adjusted appropriately, for example in drug choice or by switching intravenous to oral.
It is continued unchanged regardless
Empiric therapy is a starting point; it is adjusted once culture and other results are available.
It is always stopped completely
Results may confirm the need for treatment; the regimen is adjusted to them rather than always stopped.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set2.q: Why are infections of prosthetic implants and devices especially hard to treat?
opts: Implants release antibiotics that select resistance
Most implants release no drug; the problem is that microbes form biofilms on their surfaces.
The immune system attacks the device
An immune reaction to the device is not the stated problem; microbial biofilm formation on the surface is.
Implant infections are always viral
Implant infections are typically bacterial; what makes them hard is the biofilm that forms on the device.
Microbes form biofilms on them
Correct: prosthetic implants and devices are prone to microbial biofilm formation, which is why foreign body-associated infections are a special circumstance for antimicrobial therapy.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set2.q: A patient stops a prescribed antibiotic course as soon as they feel better. Which driver of resistance does this illustrate?
opts: Agricultural overuse
Agricultural overuse is antibiotics used in crops and livestock; stopping one's own course early is patient non-compliance.
Inappropriate prescribing
Inappropriate prescribing is the clinician's choice to give an antibiotic that is not needed; here the patient is not following the course.
Surgical prophylaxis
Surgical prophylaxis is a planned preventive dose before an operation; stopping a treatment course early is non-compliance.
Patient non-compliance
Correct: patient non-compliance, such as leaving off treatment early or against medical advice, is listed among the drivers of resistance.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set2.q: In the stewardship cycle, what should be considered before antimicrobial drugs are used?
opts: An intravenous route of delivery
Route comes later, if an antimicrobial is used at all; the cycle first weighs a non-antibiotic alternative.
A non-antibiotic alternative
Correct: after the diagnosis, the cycle asks whether a non-antibiotic alternative could prevent, control or treat the infection before antimicrobials are used.
A second broad-spectrum agent
Adding a second agent is not the stewardship step; the cycle first considers whether a non-antibiotic alternative would do.
A longer course than usual
Lengthening a course is not part of the cycle; it asks whether a non-antibiotic option could prevent, control or treat the infection.

set2.io: 2 — Describe fecal microbiota transplant (FMT)
set2.q: What makes fecal microbiota transplant more accessible as a therapy?
opts: Over-the-counter home kits
Unscreened home preparations are not the answer; stool banks of screened donors make it accessible.
Synthetic stool made in factories
The material is not synthetic: it is screened donor stool, collected and held in stool banks.
Antibiotic-treated stool
Stool is not treated with antibiotics; stool banks of screened donor samples make it accessible.
Stool banks of screened donor samples
Correct: there are stool banks to make this therapeutic option more accessible, holding screened donor stool samples.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set2.q: A patient on immunosuppressive therapy after an organ transplant is given an antimicrobial while well. What is the rationale?
opts: Treatment of a resistant superbug
No infection is present; the drug prevents infection in an immunocompromised patient, which is prophylaxis.
Desensitization to the transplanted organ
Antimicrobials do not desensitize to a graft; here they prevent infection while immunity is suppressed.
Prophylaxis in an immunocompromised patient
Correct: antimicrobial prophylaxis is used in immunocompromised patients, such as those with human immunodeficiency virus infection, cancer chemotherapy or transplant immunosuppression.
Empiric therapy for a confirmed infection
Empiric therapy treats a suspected infection in a sick patient; giving a drug to a well, immunocompromised patient is prophylaxis.

set2.io: 2 — Describe fecal microbiota transplant (FMT)
set2.q: Why is fecal microbiota transplant an alternative to another antibiotic course in recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection?
opts: It kills the patient's remaining gut bacteria
It does the opposite: it adds a healthy donor community to the gut.
It vaccinates the gut against the toxin
It is not a vaccine; it restores the commensal microflora that keeps Clostridioides difficile in check.
It restores the commensal flora the antibiotics disturbed
Correct: Clostridioides difficile infection is an indirect effect of antibiotics on the commensal microflora, and fecal transplant restores that flora rather than adding more antibiotic.
It is a stronger antibiotic
It contains no antibiotic; it restores the commensal flora that antibiotics disturbed.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set2.q: What is a hospital antibiogram mainly used for?
opts: Guiding empiric therapy
Correct: antibiograms are profiles of antimicrobial susceptibility used to guide empiric therapy, the choice made before culture results are back.
Diagnosing viral infections
Antibiograms describe bacterial susceptibility to antimicrobials; they guide empiric therapy rather than diagnose viruses.
Setting a drug's price
Cost is not what an antibiogram records; it summarizes susceptibility to guide empiric therapy.
Measuring a patient's kidney function
Kidney function is a patient measurement; an antibiogram is an organism susceptibility profile that guides empiric choices.

set2.io: 4 — Describe other alternative therapies to antibiotic use
set2.q: According to one hypothesis about cooking spices, where should spice use be heaviest?
opts: Only in coastal fishing regions
Coastline is not the variable; the hypothesis ties heavy spice use to hot climates and fast food spoilage.
In hot climates where food spoils quickly
Correct: the hypothesis is that spice use is heaviest where a hot climate goes with rapid food spoilage, because some herbs and spices kill bacteria and fungi.
In cold climates with long winters
The prediction is the reverse: hot climates with rapid food spoilage, where antimicrobial spices would help most.
Wherever refrigeration is most common
Refrigeration slows spoilage and would lessen the need; the hypothesis points to hot climates with rapid spoilage.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set2.q: Which information does a standard antibiogram leave out?
opts: The minimum inhibitory concentration
Correct: the minimum inhibitory concentration is not included, nor are patient risk factors or the effect of combining drugs.
The organism's name
The organism is the row of the table; what is left out is the minimum inhibitory concentration.
The number of isolates tested
The number tested is usually shown with each organism; the minimum inhibitory concentration is what is missing.
The percentage susceptible to each drug
Percent susceptible is the core of an antibiogram; it is the minimum inhibitory concentration that it does not give.

set2.io: 2 — Describe fecal microbiota transplant (FMT)
set2.q: Donor screening for fecal microbiota transplant is modeled on which other kind of screening?
opts: Newborn genetic screening
Genetic screening is unrelated; stool donor screening resembles blood bank screening for pathogens.
Cancer screening by colonoscopy
Colonoscopy may deliver the transplant, but donor screening is modeled on blood bank screening.
Blood bank donor screening
Correct: stool donor screening is similar to blood bank screening, to reduce the risk from blood-borne and other pathogens.
Organ transplant tissue typing
Tissue typing matches immune antigens; stool donor screening is modeled on blood bank screening for pathogens.

set2.io: 3 — Describe phage therapy
set2.q: For phage therapy, which kind of bacteriophage is needed?
opts: Any phage that infects human cells
Phages do not infect human cells, and therapy needs lytic phages that kill the target bacterium.
A phage with no genome
A phage with no genome could not replicate; therapy needs lytic phages.
A lytic phage
Correct: therapy needs lytic phages, which replicate and burst the bacterium; lysogenic phages instead fold their genome into the host.
A lysogenic phage
Lysogenic phages insert into the host and can sit there without killing it; therapy needs lytic phages that destroy the bacterium.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set2.q: Antibiotics are effective against which kind of infection?
opts: Viral infections only
Antibiotics have no effect on viruses at all; they are drugs against bacteria.
Any infection with fever
Fever accompanies viral illness too, which antibiotics cannot treat; antibiotics work only against bacterial infections.
Bacterial infections only
Correct: antibiotics treat only bacterial infections; they do nothing against viruses, which is why most colds and many sore throats do not need them.
Bacterial and viral infections
Antibiotics do not act on viruses; they treat only bacterial infections.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
set2.q: Which is a DIRECT adverse effect of an antimicrobial drug?
opts: Infection with a resistant pathogen
A raised chance of drug-resistant infection is an indirect effect; toxicity to the kidney or liver is direct.
Kidney or liver toxicity
Correct: direct adverse effects include allergy, acute or chronic toxicity such as kidney or liver toxicity, drug-drug interactions and therapeutic failure.
Clostridioides difficile infection
Clostridioides difficile infection is an INDIRECT effect, through damage to the commensal gut flora.
Antibiotics in the water supply
Effects on environmental microflora, such as antibiotics in food or water, are indirect effects.
